chapter: Second European tour and the crash
title: Jazz treatments of Tannhauser and the 1812 Overture
summary: He describes the band's modern versions of Wagner and Rimsky-Korsakov and a bells-and-cannon 1812 Overture.

blocks.x: Well, I've seen one of the programs from that concert, I guess it's from the first one, the Danish one.

And I noticed in the program you had, you were doing your versions, you very special versions, of "Tannhauser" and other things from the European classical repertoire. And I've also seen the Danish reviews, and I know that the Danes, the reviewers, were quite startled. They thought for awhile it was sacrilege. But they really loved it. But they had
never heard anything like it. And their descriptions of it are very funny and very enthusiastic. That out of all this chaos, they said, emerged suddenly Tannhauser.
And apparently, according to those reviews, the audience was just jubilant. And I wonder if, for instance, Tannhauser. Could you demonstrate on the piano how you would do any of these things.

I couldn't right now, because I don't think I would do a good job at it. But I will tell you. You see, we were using modern idioms, but at the same time the solo was sacred to us, you know what I mean?

Like, (sings Tannhauser). But at the same time, we would be using, (sings syncopated accompaniment). Things like that, with the saxophone. And it turned out well. Well, we had quite a number of them that we did. Some Rimsky-Korsakov, and one that we had was the "Overture of 1812". And we had it fixed so that you could actually hear the bells of Moscow and we had the drum beating so that now and then it was like the cannons, the Napoleonic cannons were shooting. And we did that up in a great way.
And as far as I know, nobody was doing that in this country.
Oh no. Not, no blacks anyhow.
